questions.question: Explain, with one example from each sector, why the lesson claims that the informal and formal sectors run on identical accounting concepts but differ in recording.
questions.expected_answer: Both command the same concepts: a spaza owner's R3 000 saved cash and a supermarket's R500 000 bank deposit are both capital; a fridge and a delivery vehicle are both fixed assets kept for use. The difference is that the formal business documents and records each item (accounts, source documents, statements) while the informal trader holds the same knowledge in memory and cash.

questions.question: Describe the 'leak' that appears when the spaza's month is computed from memory versus in a notebook, and what it teaches about why formal businesses record every expense.
questions.expected_answer: Memory kept only the big numbers (R4 500 in, R3 000 stock → R1 500 profit) and lost the small expenses — taxi R160, electricity R90, airtime R50 — so true profit was R1 200, not R1 500. Small expenses leak from memory and inflate apparent profit; recording them when they occur keeps the profit figure honest, which is what formal bookkeeping's discipline exists to do.

questions.question: Choose one indigenous practice from the lesson and show, in your own words, which modern accounting procedures live inside it.
questions.expected_answer: A stokvel: fixed regular contributions are capital formation; the contribution book is a ledger; the treasurer's report-back to members is financial reporting/accountability; rules about missed payments are credit control. (Equally valid: cattle as countable stored wealth = an asset register; communal grazing rules with elders checking = internal control.)
